item.title: Who Are We When the Meeting Is Over?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Who Are We When the Meeting Is Over?

What backstage conversations reveal about authenticity and safety at work.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Self-editing at work is normal, but too much can distance us from what we truly think.
  • Backstage conversations often reveal risks and concerns that official meetings leave unspoken.
  • Authenticity involves alignment between our values and behavior, rather than full disclosure.
  • Psychological safety helps people raise concerns before frustration moves into private conversations.

Recently, I was on Zoom with a colleague for a meeting that was being recorded, as so many of our meetings are these days. The official conversation ended, everyone else left, and the two of us stayed behind to talk for a few more minutes.

Oops! The Recording is still on
Source: Lindsey Godwin/ Chat GPT/ Used with permission

You probably know what happened next.

Our meeting voices disappeared, and the conversation became more candid and considerably less appropriate for broad distribution. We said things that belonged in a private exchange between trusted colleagues, including a few comments I would not want repeated, forwarded, or preserved for posterity in the cloud.

Then one of us noticed the small red recording symbol still glowing on the screen.

My body reacted before my mind assembled the facts. My stomach dropped as I frantically began mentally reviewing the previous several minutes. What exactly had I said? Had I used names? Who would receive the recording? Would anyone continue listening after the formal meeting ended? Could we delete it? Could we delete the internet?

The situation was eventually handled, but the panic stayed with me. I felt relieved that our private conversation would remain private while also wondering why the discovery had felt so exposing. The recording had captured a very real version of me. It also revealed the distance between the person I had been during the meeting and the person who appeared once I believed it was over.

Most of us make similar adjustments throughout the day, responding to the audience, the power dynamics, and the settings around us. We soften our skepticism in front of a supervisor, become more patient with a client, or wait until after a meeting to say what we actually thought.

Sociologist Erving Goffman described social life through the metaphor of theater (1959). We have front-stage settings, where we manage the impressions others form of us, and backstage settings, where we can step out of character, complain, recover, rehearse, and compare notes with the other performers. He suggested that moving between those settings is part of how people navigate different roles and social expectations.

The workplace requires some degree of performance. I do not need access to every passing thought my colleagues have, nor do they need access to mine. Some self-editing is part of working with others. Professionalism asks us to use judgment about what we share, when we share it, and how we express it.

article continues after advertisement

Still, my accidental recording left me with an uncomfortable question: How large has the gap become between our front-stage and backstage selves?

Many of us spend enormous energy editing ourselves at work, sounding more enthusiastic or certain than we really feel. The more honest conversation often begins later in the hallway, over text, or on the Zoom call we mistakenly believe has stopped recording.

Sometimes that conversation is indeed better kept private. Honesty still requires judgment about the impact of our words. Other times, however, the backstage conversation contains exactly what the meeting was missing: a risk no one named, an unrealistic workload, or an assumption no one questioned. Its power comes from the candor that the official conversation did not allow.

Research on authenticity suggests that living authentically involves knowing ourselves, seeing ourselves with reasonable clarity, acting in ways that align with our values, and allowing more of that self to appear within our relationships (Kernis & Goldman, 2006). Thinking about authenticity as alignment feels more useful than simply telling people to “bring their whole selves to work.”

I am unsure that every workplace has earned access to our whole selves. People need private spaces where they can process unfinished thoughts, seek advice, vent frustration, and make sense of their experiences with people they trust. Still, I began to wonder whether some of what appears backstage could be expressed more responsibly before the meeting ends.

My work in Appreciative Inquiry has taught me to notice how a different question can open a different possibility. My first question after the Zoom mishap was, “How do I make sure I am never caught saying something like that again?” Later, a different question occurred to me: “What would need to be true for me to say the truer thing before the meeting ended?”

article continues after advertisement

The truer thing does not have to be the rawest version of the thought. It can be expressed with care and clarity. Instead of pretending to agree, I might say, “I understand the direction, and I have a concern I have not heard us discuss.” I might ask, “Are we being realistic about the time and resources this will require?” Or perhaps, “What assumptions should we test before moving forward?”

Whether people can take such interpersonal risks depends partly on the environment around them. Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety shows that teams learn more effectively when people believe they can ask questions, acknowledge mistakes, raise concerns, and offer ideas without being humiliated or punished (1999).

What I have seen in my work is how leaders play an important role in narrowing the gap between the meeting and the meeting after the meeting. They can respond with curiosity when someone disagrees and make room for concerns that are inconvenient or unfinished. They can also pay attention when every official conversation ends in agreement, while every hallway conversation begins with, “Well, that was ridiculous.”

The rest of us can notice where we become unrecognizable to ourselves. Which rooms make us overly agreeable, polished, cautious, or silent? Where do we leave the real version of our thinking outside the door? The answers may reveal something about power and culture, as well as our own habits of avoiding discomfort, preserving approval, or waiting for someone else to speak first.

I remain deeply grateful that no one will be studying the final minutes of that recording. Private conversations have value, and informal remarks do not belong to the entire organization. I am still thinking, though, about the person who appeared when I believed the meeting was over. She was candid, funny, frustrated, imperfect, and considerably less rehearsed. Much of what she said belonged in a private conversation, though a small part of it probably needed to be said sooner and with care during the meeting.

article continues after advertisement

Authenticity does not require us to live as though the camera is always on. Perhaps it asks us to create relationships and workplaces where turning the camera on does not require us to become someone else.

item.title: The Toxic Positivity Trap and a Japanese Alternative
item.description:
Toxic Positivity

The Toxic Positivity Trap and a Japanese Alternative

Why "everything happens for a reason" can backfire and what to say instead.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Toxic positivity rushes people toward a resolution instead of letting them feel and find their way.
  • Mimamoru, a Japanese concept, means watching over someone without jumping in to fix things or direct the path.
  • Real empathy offers presence and faith in the individual, not silver linings or forced positivity.

Every time I hear someone say, "It's all happening for you, not to you," or "Everything happens for a reason," I wince. Maybe you've said these phrases, or had them said to you. Usually well-intentioned, these reassurances become a form of spiritual bypassing where spiritual or positive reframing sidesteps unresolved emotional pain (Welwood, 1984).

Believing suffering has a purpose can help people find meaning and resilience, but timing matters. For someone in deep upset, these platitudes can leave the griever feeling unseen and maybe even foolish for hurting. They push the griever toward resolution in a way that mostly helps the speaker feel more comfortable. They can leave the person on the receiving end feeling guilty and ashamed for not finding the bright side fast enough. These words offer fate instead of presence.

Spiritual bypassing can include phrases that might fit in with what is called "toxic positivity." Statements like "you'll feel better soon" or "it could be worse" can feel dismissive to someone who is hurting. Real empathy tolerates not knowing how or when things resolve. Empathy doesn't require the pain to mean something, and it doesn't compare or force a positive focus.

What Is Empathy?

Empathy has two components: the cognitive aspect, understanding another's perspective without losing your own, and the affective aspect, feeling something alongside someone who is struggling (Decety & Jackson, 2004).

Often, we imagine empathy as walking a mile in someone's shoes. But what if empathy was more about sitting with them in the mud, shoes and all, without trying to clean them off or explain why they got muddy?

Mimamoru: A Japanese Practice of Watchful Restraint

In Japanese, mimamoru means watching over a child without unnecessary interference, trusting their capacity to move through difficulty on their own (Nakatsubo et al., 2021). With mimamoru, teachers and parents resist the urge to direct or fix things for their children. This practice is found in Japanese child care, elder care, and home settings (Bamba & Haight, 2009). Japanese families learn mimamoru through experience and by watching each other do it.

article continues after advertisement

The opposite of mimamoru is lecturing, taking over, or intervening before natural consequences land. Practicing mimamoru means staying watchful and available without offering uninvited guidance. It communicates: I trust you to find your way through, and I’m here.

Western psychology has a related concept called autonomy support, from self-determination theory. With autonomy support, parents offer children choice and reasoning instead of directives, so decisions feel agentic (Ryan & Deci, 2000). Research suggests that autonomy support predicts better emotion regulation in children and preteens (Brenning et al., 2015; Matte-Gagné et al., 2015).

Addiction recovery communities have their own version of mimamoru: detaching with love. In recovery, this means remaining loving while letting someone face the consequences of their choices rather than assuming responsibility or rescuing them.

Autonomy support, mimamoru, and detaching with love all agree that stepping back, without disappearing, is itself a form of love and care. This may be the most difficult part of parenting, or even friendships. It is a practice in patience that requires presence and a willingness to listen without trying to "fix" anything.

A parent practicing mimamoru with a toddler knows the child will eventually tie their own shoes. A struggling friend may not offer the same certainty. But what if we practiced mimamoru there anyway? What if presence, trust, and restraint are the care someone really needs?

What Real Empathy Sounds Like

A dear friend once said to me, "I'm so very sorry for what you're going through. Whether you're in the depths of hell, touching the sky, or anywhere in between, I'm here for you. I have faith in you, and I'm eager to hear what you'll teach us from this." It was a voice message. Something in her tone lifted me without hyping me up; it was grounding and allowing. She made room for whatever I felt instead of asking me to feel better. I listened to her message 10 times, and later found myself repeating similar words to others.

Her words invited all my feelings, no matter how messy. The phrase "the depths of hell, touching the sky, or anywhere in between" held the entire spectrum open. She didn't guess at what I was experiencing; she was willing to stay for it all. Instead of saying, "I'm sorry, and I hope this passes soon," she said, "I'm here for all of it."

article continues after advertisement

When she said, “I have faith in you,” I felt more faith in my own capacities. She expressed a vote of confidence rather than pity. She honored my timing and a hopeful future without rushing me toward it. She expressed anticipation for what I'd learn from my grief without implying I should already be there.

My friend didn't dissolve into my pain, nor did she stand outside it. She stayed grounded and available. In Japanese terms, she mimamoru'd me.

What to Say to Someone Who Is Struggling

Many people ask me how they can help others through difficult times and what to say. When someone you love is grieving, read the words my friend said and try these three things:

  1. Pause before offering a silver lining. Acknowledge the full range of emotion instead of narrowing it. Saying "I don't know exactly where you are right now, but I'm here with you for all of it" says more than any reframe.
  2. Communicate faith, not pity. "I feel so bad for you" focuses on your discomfort, whereas "I have faith in you" honors their strength.
  3. Offer mimamoru. Watch over your friends and loved ones without intervening, and trust that steadfast, non-interfering presence is healing (Bamba & Haight, 2009).

What if mimamoru, staying steady and patient without pushing for resolution, is what real empathy actually looks like? This doesn't need a name to be practiced or a position of superiority to be offered. It simply asks us to be in the mud alongside those we care about, and to trust them to walk out in their own time and their own way.

item.title: Say Hello to Your Brain
item.description:
Neuroscience

Say Hello to Your Brain

A basic understanding of the brain can increase insight and lead to real change.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Basic knowledge about the brain can yield greater understanding and compassion about mental health issues.
  • Considering the roles played by different parts of the brain play can reduce mental health stigma.
  • Tapping into different parts of the brain and their function can help unlock creativity.
Source: Hainguyenrp/Pixabay

Have you ever tried to do something and failed, only to have someone say, "Try harder," or "Use more willpower?" If you have, chances are that didn't help, and possibly only made you feel worse? Well-intentioned or not, that type of suggestion reveals a profound lack of knowledge about how the brain works, and not only does it impede finding solutions, but it may also lead to self-blame and stigma around mental health and illness.

For example, using one's willpower means, in neuroscience terms, tapping into the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain that governs what is called executive function. The "CEO" of the brain, this area considers the big picture, plans, organizes, and inhibits impulsive actions. If one's problem is due to not being able to plan or direct action, then the prefrontal cortex may be the target of the solution.

However, most emotional and behavioral issues involve other parts of the brain primarily, or in concert with one another. As a clinical psychologist, I have often seen addiction viewed as a problem of lack of control (again, the prefrontal cortex), when the more "primitive" parts—not the cortex—of the brain are at work. Addiction often involves traumatic memories stored in the amygdala, the area from which fear emanates, as those who struggle with it often use substances to cope with these memories. The more this is understood, the more compassionate we can be, and the more likely that efforts to change will target the parts of the brain that bring about healing.

Source: Mahmood Sufian/Pexels

While most people know a lot about the different muscles of the body and how to exercise them, fewer probably know about the different parts of the brain.

The brain is a remarkable organ, exquisitely shaped by millions of years of human evolution. Any mind-altering drugs taken in from the outside the body work precisely because the brain has the capacity, in the form of specific neurotransmitters, circuits, and receptors, to make them work. An opiate-based high mimics the action of naturally occurring endorphins; anti-anxiety drugs lower the reactivity of the amygdala and the central nervous system, but this also occurs when one activates the language centers in the cortex by speaking or writing ("I am scared"), which simultaneously diminishes the reactivity of the emotional parts of the brain.

What about commonly known strategies for improving well-being, such as exercise or eating salmon? While most of us know that they enhance mood and prevent depression, knowing the underlying neurobiology can bring clarity and a sense of agency. We can control what we eat and whether to work out. (Exercise releases endorphins, inhibiting pain and providing a sense of well-being, or "runner's high"; salmon contains the building blocks for serotonin, which regulates mood, as well as reduces inflammation, which research shows is a major underlying factor in many psychological and physical disorders.)

article continues after advertisement
Source: Tara Winstead/Pexels

Creativity, too, can benefit from knowledge about the brain. Writers, for example, often complain of being "stuck" or experiencing "writer's block." Exercises to unlock creativity often ask the writer to utilize all their senses rather than just the visual, or to create with the nondominant hand. These types of exercise simply tap into underused parts of the brain to open up areas of inspiration.

For example, the writer naturally relies on the language centers in the left temporal lobe, but visual images, smells, and emotional memories all reside in other parts of the brain, and accessing them can add emotion and depth to writing. And switching from your right hand to the left would stimulate the right hemisphere of the cortex (the brain is contralateral to the body), which houses spatial and holistic abilities. Applying such knowledge might reduce frustration and procrastination among writers and other creatives waiting for their well-worn circuits to rejuvenate.

Source: Delta Works/Pixabay

So go ahead, get acquainted with your own self-sustaining, beautiful brain. You don't need to be a neuroscientist to benefit from learning a few basic concepts. The best way to start is by learning the major structures of the brain: the parts of the hindbrain, the midbrain, and the cerebral cortex, and their functions. Then, if you wish, go deeper into the molecular level to the major neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine, GABA, etc.) and how they work (synapses, receptors). It is truly fascinating, and understanding the fundamentals can play a role in fixing whatever ails and providing fresh inspiration.

Your brain will thank you for it.

item.title: The Art of Remarrying the Same Person
item.description:
Marriage

The Art of Remarrying the Same Person

Lessons from wise elders and fifty years of marriage.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Lasting marriage thrive on tolerance, kindness, and respect for differences.
  • Strong couples balance intimacy with independence as they grow together.
  • Curiosity, humor, and generosity help repair inevitable relationship ruptures.
  • Love endures when partners embrace each other's imperfections with wisdom.

The challenges of a marriage are obvious. Two people, with differences, set out on a course of connection. It’s a partnership to last for years through developmental changes and the ups and downs of life. According to data from the National Center for Family and Marriage Research, only about 6 to 8 percent of all married couples will reach their 50th golden anniversary.

Source: Hector Reyes/Unsplash

What’s their secret? Is there wisdom regarding how to age a marriage like a fine wine? What can those setting out or those already on their journey learn from them? Combing through interviews with wise elder psychoanalysts who had achieved long-term relationships, some very salient points are clear. All of which I can attest to as someone who has also achieved the magic golden 50 years.

Philosopher Stanley Cavell noted that “All good marriages are re-marriages.” Why? Psychoanalyst Theodore Reik long ago suggested that the person we marry is our “ego ideal,” the person who embodies what we desire yet lack. Over time, we find that our partner is not our ideal and can get disillusioned. It is here that the seeds of a long-term relationship can really take off and grow. The honeymoon is over; you wonder how you ever got into this and whether you should ride it out. Like Humpty Dumpty, our marriages falter; the goal is to put them back together again and go forward differently.

Research shows that wisdom is related to how people achieve long-term relationships. Let’s think about the components of wisdom: It’s pragmatic, includes paradoxes (though balanced), and is built on kindness, humility, and a deep regard for the other. The pragmatism of marriage is obvious: it’s a division of labor, a practical compatibility with complementary skills.

What about the balanced paradox or the kindness?

In marriage, as in all intimate relationships, we are separate and attached. But intimacy and dependency can be balanced, on one side of a teeter-totter with autonomy and feeling that one can go on without the other—we balance being separate and being attached.

In remarriage, Cavell notes that proportion is key. It is both the balance of self and other and one’s emotional state. The wise person has the capacity for “affect optimization,” an ability to hold positive and negative feelings about something or someone while emphasizing the positive over the negative. Psychoanalyst Marvin Hurvich, Ph.D., defined it this way: The attempt to understand the mate, the attempt to put yourself in the mate’s place, and the attempt to fall back on the enduring positive aspects of the relationship during rocky episodes or times.

Interviews with wise elders yielded some specific suggestions, each embodying one or more aspects of wisdom. Among the suggestions were:

  • Give each other space to do your own thing and be interested in the other.
  • Take care of each other, be on each other’s team.
  • Be dependable.
  • Have respect and common interests other than the children.
  • Share values important to you both.
  • Have a sense of humor.
  • Be curious about your partner’s internal world.

And from my own 50-year marriage, I’ll add:

  • Be generous of spirit: When you are at fault, apologize and be the first to extend an olive branch; bring you and your partner back into connection.

Accepting the otherness of the other is a consistent theme in the golden anniversary group. If love languages differ—for example, for one it is acts of service and for the other, words of affirmation—give your partner what floats their boat and not your own.

The surprising one word that wise elders used more than any other when describing successful long-term relationships was tolerance. Tolerance for our differences. Tolerance for those little annoyances. Developing the capacity to see the big picture and accepting the limits of your partner are key. The road is never a (boring) smooth highway, but the gifts of maturation are plenty. The best wedding gift of 50 or so years? Looking back on the vista of a shared history. Being both witness and participant for decades upon decades with a chosen other can’t be understated.

item.title: Building Inner Conviction in Unstable Times
item.description:
Friends

Building Inner Conviction in Unstable Times

The art of friendship might provide some solid ground for our kids, and us, too.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Young people are describing pervasive numbness, lack of motivation, and an absence of drive or purpose.
  • Their struggles reflect the fragmenting of the social values and truths on which inner conviction depends.
  • Learning to be a friend might provide them, and us, some firm footing.

Feelings of emptiness and estrangement seem to be spreading in contemporary society, especially among the young. Why this is happening was the basis for an article, “A Brief History of Purpose-Seeking,” that I published in the January/February 2026 issue of Psychology Today. Not long after it came out, I received an astute letter from Sobia Mahmood, a Toronto-based registered psychotherapist, who gave me permission to quote it. She said she felt compelled to write because the article “articulated something I’ve been observing clinically for some time.”

Source: Zizi_zi / Unsplash

Ms. Mahmood explains: “I work with children and adolescents, as well as adults, and increasingly I find myself sitting with young teens who describe pervasive numbness, lack of motivation, and an absence of drive or purpose. What stands out is that some of these youth do not identify a clear history of trauma or deprivation; some have supportive families and considerable intellectual capacity.”

She then gives the type of example that many other people who work with youth have reported: “a bright adolescent who knows she could excel academically if she applied herself, yet she sees little meaning or value in doing so and reports feeling this way since early childhood. She often questions the point of conventional paths such as a 9-to-5 career, sentiments that echo much of the discourse circulating on social media.”

Following on one of the points in the article, Ms. Mahmood also wonders if what she is “seeing clinically reflects a fragmentation or erosion of the internalized convictions that once helped structure identity and purpose.” Such inner convictions, I argued in “Brief History,” require external and stable reference points, which are increasingly unavailable. Now, young people, Ms. Mahmood rightly observes, are often forced to navigate amid “rapidly shifting and often contradictory value systems.”

Picking up on this thread, I want to reflect on the need for stable reference points, the lack of which leaves people, like Ms. Mahmood’s clients, feeling empty and adrift.

Everything Has Become a Question

What, we might ask, does a coherent, vital sense of self require? At a minimum, we need our actions, our convictions, and our life direction to make sense to us, and to see them as meaningful and harmoniously interconnected. An understanding of right and wrong is also essential, and the confidence that we can choose between them. Capacities like these, in turn, require a supporting structure. We can’t lead good lives, find our identity, and be of service to others without some fixed social coordinates, some solid ground of truth and values to stand on, and so orient ourselves to the world. As psychoanalyst Allen Wheelis once wrote: “[I]f everything is open to question, no question can be answered.”1

The problem for many is that nearly everything is open to question. Consider this simple example. In her book Alone Together, sociologist Sherry Turkle notes that preteen girls in the late 1980s and early 1990s were wearing clothes so provocative that the style was called “baby harlot.” Their boomer parents, who grew up rejecting parental rules, didn’t know where to draw lines. But what they did know, Turkle observes, is that there were rules. “One might say,” she writes, “it is the job of teenagers to complain about constraints and the job of parents to insist on them, even if the rules are not obeyed.”2

Now, however, the rules themselves have gone missing. This is not to say that all values and standards have disappeared. The change, rather, is that the old certainties, which had previously been taken for granted as matters of pre-reflective routine, have broken up. Rules, truths, roles, and standards, like the parental authority and values the boomer generation was subject to, have lost their self-evident quality. They are no longer authoritative and socially constitutive. Now, everything must be taken up and negotiated as questions, such as about age-appropriate dress, by individuals and in the context of their private lives.

Up for discussion and in need of justification, the now fragmented rules and values provide no consistent orienting compass in matters small (appropriate dress) or great (future direction). Teenagers are marooned, as in Turkle’s example, unable, she found, to “easily articulate any rules about sexual conduct except for those that will keep them ‘safe.’”

A lack of specific guidance is one consequence. Another, deeper outcome follows from the loss of firm structures of rules, values, and standards. Young people (all of us) have little they can really count on. Without a definite shape, social life loses its objective quality and appears arbitrary: ambivalent, inconsistent, and contradictory. Deciding everything seems like freedom as the old rules have lost their grip. But choosing is precarious—failure, the wrong choice, is always an immediate possibility—and deprives experience of any intrinsic meaning or ultimate value or purpose. The world becomes more like a mirror, merely reflecting back one’s own fears and desires.

Young people are facing a social void, where their concerns can find no settled response. Many are left feeling empty, unmotivated, and without conviction.

Finding Some Footing

Psychotherapist Mahmood’s letter ends with a request. If the “broader social foundations” are increasingly unstable, how might those “working with children and adolescents help [them] build a sense of ‘firm footing’”? This is not an easy question to answer. If it were, the problem would have already been addressed, or we would not have abandoned or failed to maintain the stable structures in the first place. The hard reality is that we are in a new situation. Once upended, established customs, traditions, moral codes, and the like cannot be restored to the realm of the tacitly believed and understood. We have no choice now but to choose.

No big program will help us. If we are to make a space out of which commitments can grow, we might begin by cultivating the art of friendship and the habits of the heart that make friendship possible. This art is a tradition, going back at least to the reflections of Plato and Aristotle on philia, and continuing ever since.

The forces of fragmentation, however, have been at work. Many today have few friends; many describe the friendships they do have as shallow, superficial, and unreliable. Numerous are the barriers and obstacles to the practice of friendship and hospitality. In a recent post, for instance, I noted the rise of a new ethic of self. With the loss of routine and culturally shared guides to action, we are now pressed, institutionally and as a kind of moral duty, to make choices about our life and goals based on our private self-interest. Such an ethic is poor soil for the growth of friendship, both in terms of being present to the best interest of others and knowing what we have to offer in friendship with them.

But the art is alive, and we can learn, and teach others, how to be a good friend. The hunger is there. People want to be known and loved for their own sake, to be heard, to be in conversation, to be needed. In nurturing friendship, we find virtue and push back against the tyranny of our contemporary preoccupation with self. In these fluid times, it can provide some stable ground on which to develop commitments we can stand by.

item.title: When Language Disappears, Thought Remains
item.description:
Cognition

When Language Disappears, Thought Remains

A new study confirms what Frank Muldowney has known for 40 years.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Logical reasoning and language live in separate parts of the brain.
  • Losing language does not mean losing the ability to think.
  • Aphasia is widely mistaken for a loss of intelligence.
The top drawing represents how Frank Muldowney sees language—as the black monolith that keeps humans and source apart. However, he emphasizes that joy, love, and emotions are our real language. The bottom drawing represents how he sees the inner journey, where the real answers are.
Source: Frank Muldowney / Used with permission

In 2024, Frank Muldowney won the lottery. Not the financial kind.

He finally learned, nearly four decades after brain surgery at the age of 19, that he had Wernicke's aphasia. This condition affects language comprehension and production, caused in his case by an arteriovenous malformation that burst in 1985.

"It felt like winning the lottery," he told me, "because my whole life suddenly made sense."

Frank reached out to me recently through LinkedIn. He is currently writing a book about his experience, the first time, he says, he has truly been able to put his thoughts into words. What he shared with me in our written exchange stopped me more than once.

What 1985 Took and What It Didn't

Frank was 19 when the surgery changed his relationship with language. In the weeks and months that followed, words sounded like noise. He couldn't read. The world stopped making sense through language, and so he went somewhere else.

"I went inward to escape the confusion," he said, "and the silence became my friend."

What happened inside that silence is the part most people, including the medical professionals around him at the time, didn't understand.

"I never felt that I had lost my ability to think," Frank told me. "I lost the language I had used to communicate my thoughts. Language began to feel like a human-made tool, while my thinking came naturally through my senses. It was like comparing a bicycle to walking. The bicycle is useful, but walking is part of who we are."

What the Science Now Confirms

A study published this month in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) by researchers at MIT and colleagues found, using both brain imaging and direct work with aphasia patients, that logical reasoning and language are handled by entirely separate neural systems (Kean et al., 2026). The brain's language network showed no meaningful engagement during formal reasoning tasks. Patients with severe aphasia, who had lost significant language function, reasoned just as accurately as people without aphasia.

Frank didn't need a brain scanner to know this. He lived it.

"My thinking became different," he said. "I lived in the present, and time felt more like a circle than a straight line. All my senses magnified and became my true language. Instead of depending on man-made linear sentences, I understood the world through images, feelings, rhythm and intuition."

The Gap Between Understanding and Speaking

One of the most striking things Frank described is something the PNAS study can confirm neurologically but cannot fully capture: what it actually feels like to have a thought that language cannot reach.

"There was a vast void between what I experienced and what I could express," he said. "I knew there was far more inside me than words could ever describe. For me, the pauses between words often carry more meaning than what is spoken or typed."

This gap had consequences far beyond communication. His family, trying to care for a 19-year-old who had been told he had brain damage, didn't know how to reach him. In the 1980s, understanding of aphasia was limited, and the confusion between losing language and losing intelligence was nearly universal.

"Subconsciously, our normal emotions had switched off," Frank said, "leaving a void between us."

He drifted. Epilepsy arrived. He found other languages: music, drawing, dance, silent films, pilgrimages through Spain, France, and Peru, where walking through nature for weeks became, as he put it, "another language."

Why He Is Writing the Book

Frank eventually discovered that more than 12 million people worldwide live with aphasia. Many, he believes, are in the same position he was in for almost 40 years: unable to fully express themselves, and unaware that millions of others share that experience.

"Writing my book became my way of helping to restore that balance," he told me. "It was my chance to give a voice to people whose thoughts often remain hidden behind the struggle to communicate."

On what he would say to someone at the beginning of this journey, Frank was characteristically precise. "Don't let other people decide what you're capable of," he said. "Because they only see your words, not your mind."

What This Means Beyond Aphasia

Frank's story is not only about aphasia. It is about something most of us have experienced in smaller, quieter ways: the feeling of knowing something before we can say it, of understanding more than our words quite reach, of thinking in images or emotions or sensations that language arrives at second.

The neuroscience now tells us this isn't metaphor. It is how the brain works.

"Thought itself is much bigger," Frank said. "Sometimes I experience an image, a feeling, or a rhythm long before I can find the words for it."

His value, he told me, has never depended on how easily he can speak. Neither, it turns out, does his thinking.

item.title: Does the World Seem Broken? Maybe That’s the Point
item.description:
Resilience

Does the World Seem Broken? Maybe That’s the Point

Accepting yourself and others can be the foundation for meaningful change.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Our distrust and fear have produced a heightened anxiety within us.
  • Self-acceptance increases your chances of being accepted by others.
  • When you accept your emotions and the reality in which you are living, you access your capacity for change.
  • Acceptance is worth your time, for the inner peace and social connections it enables.

“We just can’t continue like this,” a friend told me the other day. His six words succinctly encapsulate what many people around the world are feeling right now.

No matter which side of the political fence you hang your hat on, let me take a wild guess: You almost never speak to those on the other side.

Growth begins within.
Source: Marcos Paulo Prado / Unsplash

In fact, political polarization is at its worst since the Civil War. “A man hears what he wants to hear,” noted Simon & Garfunkel in their classic song “The Boxer,” “and disregards the rest.”

The resulting distrust and fear have produced a heightened anxiety—an emotion associated with an existential threat that’s challenging to identify while you are experiencing it—in regular citizens that’s compromising their health.

How does this happen? In high doses, the anxiety emerging within you threatens your immune system, causing it to over-produce proinflammatory cytokine (one of the immune system’s defenses to biological threats).

How Could You?

“We cannot think of being acceptable to others,” the human rights activist Malcolm X once shared, “until we have first proven acceptable to ourselves.” Numerous studies over the past century corroborate the human rights leader’s words and the strong correlation between an individual’s capacity to accept themselves as they are and to accept others as they are.

The father of client-centered therapy and former president of the American Psychological Association, Carl Rogers, would likely have agreed on this point with Malcolm X. Rogers observed that individuals accepting of themselves are more likely to be accepting of others.

Connection begins with acceptance.
Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

In fact, numerous studies have found self-acceptance and acceptance of others to be positively correlated. In our unprecedentedly polarized society, never has it been more important for you to accept others with political views, economic possibilities, or social convictions different from your own.

This acceptance can lead not only to your creating or joining more inclusive social movements, but also to the formation of unlikely friendships as you stop judging people based on one dimension of who they are and become open to all the other dimensions that make them unique human beings.

Transcending Oppression

Refusing to accept your life as it is—with the diversity of people who populate it—or others as they are lies at the root of racism, sexism, classism, and most of the other isms. If you want to be more accepting of others, then, it’s imperative that you begin by being more accepting of yourself, beginning with the feelings that emerge within you.

A study by Emory University psychologist Yara Mekawi of how over 400 African-American patients in a community hospital cope with racism found that those who acknowledged the discrimination they had experienced, shared it with others, and took actions to dismantle racism in their community did not experience long-term depressive symptoms and posttraumatic stress. The patients who passively accepted racism by keeping it to themselves and not taking any action, on the other hand, were susceptible to these detrimental long-term symptoms.

It All Begins With You

Accepting yourself as you are is the first step not only to being accepted by others as you are, but also to accepting others as they are. However, research has found that while accepting yourself is highly correlated with accepting others, it is not correlated with being accepted by others; in other words, some people will not accept you regardless of your level of self-acceptance.

Whether others are accepting of you or not in any particular social group (i.e., a group of friends, in the workplace), practicing acceptance is worth your time. Why? It diminishes the negative emotional states that result from fighting against a changed life situation that you would rather do anything other than confront.

Inner peace Is worth your time.
Source: Dingzeyu Li / Unsplash

While acceptance is not easy, it’s not optional. When you accept your emotions and the reality in which you are living, you access the power to work toward changing both. By accepting the people around you, you open your heart to a more inclusive approach to life that enables new friendships and opportunities.

Acceptance is worth your time, both for the inner peace it enables within you and the social connections it enables with others.
